Empirical Research Plan – Public vs. Private Natural-Gas Producers

============================================================
1. Identification Strategy
------------------------------------------------------------
I use two complementary designs, both variants of “differences-in-differences” (DID):

A. Price Elasticity DID  
   •  Exploit temporal shocks in the nation-wide real well-head gas price (P_t).  
   •  Compare how investment of the same firm responds to ΔP_t, and whether the response differs by listing status.

B. Staggered Shale-Discovery Triple-Difference (DDD)  
   •  “Treatment” is the arrival of a commercially viable shale play in a county-year (c,t).  
   •  Compare treated counties to never-treated counties, pre- vs. post-discovery, and public vs. private firms.  
   •  Identification uses variation across (i) space, (ii) time, and (iii) listing status.

These designs are appropriate because:  
•  Output price shocks and shale discoveries are plausibly exogenous to an individual, sub-scale producer.  
•  Firms of both listing types operate side-by-side in the same counties, satisfying the DID requirement that counterfactuals face similar environments.  
•  The rich panel (1997–2012) permits firm and county fixed effects, saturating most unobserved heterogeneity.

============================================================
2. Treatment and Control Definitions
------------------------------------------------------------
A. Price Elasticity DID  
   •  Treatment variable: interaction Public_i × lnPrice_t.  
   •  Control: Private firms’ response to lnPrice_t.  
   •  Timing: weekly price is collapsed to fiscal year averages (t). No discrete event date is needed.

B. Shale DDD  
   •  First difference: Post_ct = 1 for county-years after the first shale well is drilled in county c.  
   •  Second difference: ShaleCounty_c = 1 if county ever receives shale play.  
   •  Third difference: Public_i = 1 if firm is listed on a U.S. exchange during year t.  
   •  The key regressor is Public_i × ShaleCounty_c × Post_ct.  
   •  Control units: (i) private firms in shale counties, (ii) both firm types in never-shale counties, and (iii) the pre-period.

No running variable or cutoff is required because we are not using an RDD.

============================================================
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------------------------------------
A1.  Parallel trends (Price design): In the absence of listing-status differences, investment of public and private firms would react identically to price movements.  
      Plausibility: Firms face identical spot prices and costs; no reason public firms alone foresee price moves.

A2.  Common pre-trends (Shale DDD): Prior to shale discovery, investment trends are the same across (public, private) × (future-shale, never-shale) groups.  
      Plausibility: Shale locations were driven by geology, not by prior performance of public firms.

A3.  Exogeneity of shocks:  
      •  Price_t is set in a national market; an individual firm is tiny relative to aggregate supply.  
      •  Discovery timing is driven by large integrated service companies and advances in fracking, unrelated to local listing mix.

A4.  SUTVA / no spillovers: Drilling by one firm does not mechanically change the opportunities of another within the same county-year after conditioning on price and shale dummies. Given the vast reserves and rig availability, crowd-out is minimal.

============================================================
4. Main Threats and Mitigations
------------------------------------------------------------
T1.  Differential anticipation of shale plays.  
     •  Test: Event-study leads; coefficients on Public×Lead_k should be ≈0.  
     •  Mitigation: Drop observations 2 years pre-discovery (“donut”) and show robustness.

T2.  Time-varying financing conditions (e.g., credit-cycle shocks) that correlate with being public.  
     •  Include year×state fixed effects, and directly control for county-year bank-lending growth (FDIC data).  
     •  Alternative: Instrument external-finance capacity with national equity-market returns interacted with firm leverage (Hadlock-Pierce score).

T3.  Twoway-FE bias in staggered adoption.  
     •  Use Sun & Abraham (2020) or Callaway & Sant’Anna (2021) estimators instead of naive twoway FE for the shale design.

============================================================
5. R Code Outline
------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)    # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)        # regressions with high-dim FE
library(did)           # Callaway & Sant’Anna estimator
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load & Merge -----------------------------------------------------------
rig  <- fread("rig_count.csv")          # well-level
firm <- fread("firm_listing.csv")       # firm characteristics
price<- fread("eia_gas_price.csv")      # monthly price
shale<- fread("shale_discovery.csv")    # county-level dates

# 2. Construct Panel --------------------------------------------------------
# Aggregate wells to firm–county–year panel
rig[, year := year(spud_date)]
panel <- rig[, .(
  wells_new = .N,
  cap_stock = sum(year >= (year-3))     # simplistic cap stock
), by = .(firm_id, county, year)]

panel <- merge(panel, firm, by = "firm_id")
panel <- merge(panel, shale, by = "county", all.x = TRUE)
panel <- merge(panel, price, by = "year")

# Listing status
panel[, public := as.integer(listing_status == "public")]

# Shale post dummy
panel[, post_shale := as.integer(year >= shale_start_year & !is.na(shale_start_year))]
panel[, ever_shale := as.integer(!is.na(shale_start_year))]

# 3. Main Specification -----------------------------------------------------
# (A) Price Elasticity DID
spec_price <- feols(
  wells_new ~ ln_price * public + ln_price + log(cap_stock) |
  firm_id + year, data = panel, cluster = ~firm_id)

# (B) Shale Triple Diff with Sun & Abraham
panel[, treat_time := ifelse(ever_shale==1, shale_start_year, 0L)]
sa <- att_gt(yname = "wells_new",
             tname = "year",
             idname = "firm_id",
             gname = "treat_time",
             xformla = ~ public,
             clustervars = "firm_id",
             data = panel[year >= 1999])          # example start year
agg_sa <- aggte(sa, type = "dynamic")
# Plot event study
ggplot(data = data.frame(agg_sa$egt, agg_sa$att.egt, agg_sa$se.egt),
       aes(x = agg_sa$egt, y = agg_sa$att.egt)) +
  geom_point() + geom_errorbar(aes(ymin=att.egt-1.96*se.egt,
                                   ymax=att.egt+1.96*se.egt))

# 4. Robustness: Donut around shale arrival -------------------------------
panel_rb <- panel[abs(year - shale_start_year) > 1 | is.na(shale_start_year)]
spec_rb <- feols(
  wells_new ~ ln_price*public + ln_price + post_shale*public*ever_shale |
  firm_id + county + year, data = panel_rb, cluster = ~county)
```

============================================================
6. Expected Results
------------------------------------------------------------
Economic intuition:  
•  Access to deep public-equity markets should lessen financing constraints.  
•  Shale wells are 7–9× more capital-intensive → Prediction: Public firms increase drilling significantly more than private firms once shale arrives.  
•  Magnitude: If private firms drill 0.5 additional wells per $1 increase in gas price, public firms might drill 0.8 (β_Public×Price ≈ 0.3).  
•  For shale, public firms may raise drilling by ~25-30 % relative to baseline, while private response is modest (~5 %). The DDD coefficient should thus be ≈ 0.20-0.25 (log points).

============================================================
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID / DDD)
------------------------------------------------------------
C1 : No differential pre-trends  ………… 1  
C2 : Exogenous, well-timed treatment … 1  
C3 : Stable unit treatment value ……... 0.5 (some local spillovers possible)  
C4 : No simultaneous confounders …….. 0.5  
C5 : Proper inference with staggered … 1  

Total ≈ 4/5 → Credible but not bullet-proof; needs careful robustness work.
